A fast assistant drafts text and a stronger model verifies it. During verification, the assistant prepares drafts for possible next-round outcomes; a correct prediction makes the next draft immediately available.
Tv: verification time; Td: drafting time; h: probability the matching draft is ready; To: coordination overhead. This is our educational latency equation, not Saguaro’s complete performance model.

Predict verification outcomes, including accepted-prefix length and bonus token, and prepare their continuations on other resources during verification.
Use the matching continuation when the result arrives; otherwise take a fallback path.

Do you need text completion, an instruction-following assistant, or answers from company documents? Try a pretrained model first and define success cases, cost, and latency metrics. Training from scratch differs from connecting an interface to a model.
Write 30 representative test cases and define correctness before starting.
Prepare data and separate testing

Collect text you may use and remove duplication, corruption, and unwanted information. Split training, validation, and test sets by document or source before chunking so one document cannot leak across splits.
Train on train, select settings on validation, and open test only for final evaluation.
Turn text into tokens

A tokenizer converts text into IDs. Character tokenization is easy to learn; many models use subword units such as BPE. Reuse a pretrained model’s tokenizer when adapting it; changing vocabulary without adjusting embeddings breaks compatibility.
Try English or Arabic text below. A token need not be a word; Arabic diacritics can add tokens.
Build a causal Transformer

Each token receives an embedding and position information, followed by attention and MLP layers with residual connections and normalization. A causal mask blocks future tokens. A language head produces scores for each vocabulary token.
In the code: token and position → masked layers → norm → head. Start small to verify the training loop.
Train on the next token

Inputs are token sequences; targets are shifted one token ahead. Compute loss and gradients, then update weights over batches. Do not expose future tokens to attention or update weights during validation.
Example input: “I am learning”; targets are the following tokens. Monitor training and validation losses; only lower training loss may mean memorization.
Adapt behavior when needed

Pretraining learns text completion. SFT uses instruction-answer examples with the correct chat template; loss may be restricted to assistant responses. LoRA trains small updates instead of all weights but does not eliminate base-model computation.
Select architecture-compatible LoRA layers; save adapters, tokenizer, and the base model name and version.
Evaluate quality before scaling

Use validation loss and perplexity under the same tokenization, then task, language, instruction-following, and accuracy tests. Do not directly compare perplexity across vocabularies. Review human samples, latency, and memory while retaining the baseline.
If the model fails, inspect data, leakage, masking, and learning rate before buying larger hardware.
Save and serve the model

Save weights, configuration, tokenizer, and dependency versions. Generate by feeding context, choosing a token, and appending it until stopping. Add length limits, cost monitoring, and regression tests; finishing training does not make a reliable service.
Start locally, then compare batching, KV caching, and quantization at your required quality.
